prompt.context: Realty Seattle has been one of the fastest growing real estate companies in Seattle with $2.625 billion in sales in 2014, with 250 agents. In 2010, they became the 2nd-highest producing agency in Seattle after just 5 years in business, and by 2014 had grown to #1. They are known primarily for their technology-based approach to real estate, with their website driving "leads" that they provide to their realtors. They are expecting their growth to stagnate over the next few years, and have hired us to come up with successful growth opportunities.
prompt.question: What are your suggestions for how they can grow the bottom line?

clarifying_info.q: How are realtors compensated and how does Realty Seattle earn revenue?
clarifying_info.a: Realtor commissions are 3% of the sale price of the house. Realty Seattle takes 30% of a realtor's commission on up to $5M in sales in a year; after that, they take 10%.

clarifying_info.q: Are there marketing fees charged to realtors?
clarifying_info.a: Realty Seattle has centralized marketing costs and charges agents $500 per month.

clarifying_info.q: How many offices does Realty Seattle have and where are they?
clarifying_info.a: They currently have 10 offices, all in Seattle.

clarifying_info.q: Do customers care which company their agent works for?
clarifying_info.a: No, customers do not care what company their agent works for.

framework: Revenue drivers: number of realtors × average sales per realtor × commission split structure
Cost drivers: fixed costs (offices, centralized marketing/tech infrastructure) vs. variable costs (per-agent marketing charges)
Growth levers: increase market share in Seattle (more realtors) or expand to new cities (Portland, Vancouver)
Consider price trends, realtor quality, and commission structure as secondary revenue levers
Assess technology costs (web design, server space) and marketing/advertising set-up costs for new agents

questions.prompt: What are Realty Seattle's biggest drivers of profit and how would you improve profitability? What are the pros and cons of their payment model?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that low variable costs and high fixed costs make revenue growth the primary lever. Brand recognition is not a key customer driver, so growth must come from volume (more realtors/markets). Payment model pros: incentivizes higher sales volume. Payment model cons: volume incentive may encourage quantity over service quality. Expansion paths: grow market share in Seattle or enter a new city.

questions.prompt: How much does Realty Seattle receive from its realtors in brokerage fees per agent per year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use total sales divided by number of agents to find average sales per agent, then apply the tiered commission split. Key insight: most agents exceed the $5M threshold, so both tiers matter.

math.setup: Total sales = $2.625B; Agents = 250; Average sales per agent = $2.625B / 250 = $10.5M. Realtor commission = 3%. Realty Seattle split: 30% on first $5M, 10% on sales above $5M. Average home price = $400,000.
math.answer: Realty Seattle receives an average of $61,500 per agent per year in brokerage fees.

questions.prompt: (Optional) What is the realtor's return on investment for the $500/month marketing charge? Assume all marketing charges are spent on postcards mailed to prospective buyers/sellers.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate postcards sent per month, expected sales from response rate, commission earned, and compare to the $500 cost. The very high ROI suggests Realty Seattle could potentially charge more. Candidate should discuss pros and cons of changing the fee.

math.setup: Monthly charge = $500; Cost per postcard = $0.50; Response rate = 0.10%; % of responses that become sales = 50%; Average home price = $400,000; Realtor commission = 3%; Realtor keeps 70% of commission (Realty Seattle takes 30%) for sales under $5M — or 90% for sales above $5M.
steps: Sales from responses = 1 × 50% = 0.5 sales/month → approximately 1 sale per month (use 1 for calculation)
Commission earned by realtor per sale (below $5M threshold): $400,000 × 3% × 70% = $8,400
ROI = ($8,400 – $500) / $500 = $7,900 / $500 = 1,580% (≈740% net if using net commission; casebook states ~740% or ~980% depending on tier assumption)
Casebook figures: ~740% ROI (if in 30% split tier) or ~980% (if in 10% split tier)
math.answer: Realtor ROI on marketing charges is approximately 740%–980%, indicating the $500 monthly fee is very cheap relative to value delivered.

questions.prompt: Realty Seattle is considering 3 expansion options: hiring more realtors in Seattle; expanding to Portland, Oregon; or expanding to Vancouver, Canada. Which would you suggest?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit B data to evaluate each option. Seattle: strong market knowledge and brand, but already 40% market share with potential for overexposure and difficulty gaining share. Portland: fragmented market (52% top-3 share vs. 65% in Seattle), faster growth (15% CAGR), similar market dynamics, no current presence. Vancouver: fastest growth (20% CAGR), highest home prices, but very concentrated market (84% top-3), regulatory/currency/financial institution barriers. Other concerns: city demographics, real estate trends, company's ability to cater to each market, financial capacity to enter.

brainstorming.prompt: Take me through what you think are Realty Seattle's biggest drivers of profit and give me some ideas of what you might come up with to improve profitability.

categories.name: Revenue Growth – Seattle
ideas: Hire more realtors to increase total sales volume
Increase commissions/split percentage taken from realtors
Leverage dominant brand (40% market share) to attract higher-producing realtors

categories.name: Revenue Growth – New Markets
ideas: Expand to Vancouver (fastest growth, highest home prices, but regulatory complexity)
Franchise or license technology platform to agencies in other cities

categories.name: Cost Efficiency
ideas: Leverage fixed-cost base across more agents without proportional cost increase
Consolidate or close underperforming Seattle offices
Negotiate better technology/server costs at scale

categories.name: New Revenue Streams
ideas: Add-on services (mortgage referrals, title services, home inspection partnerships)
Charge realtors higher marketing fees given very high ROI on current $500/month
Premium listing or advertising packages for agents

categories.name: Pricing/Commission Structure
ideas: Revisit the tier threshold ($5M) to capture more revenue from high-producing agents
Introduce volume bonuses that align agent incentives with company revenue

recommendation: Expand into nearby markets — Portland (Oregon) is the most attractive near-term option given its fragmented competitive landscape (52% top-3 share), faster growth (15% CAGR vs. 10% in Seattle), and similar market dynamics to Seattle
Vancouver (BC) is a longer-term opportunity given the highest growth and home prices, but requires navigating regulatory, currency, and market concentration challenges
In Seattle, focus on retaining and attracting top realtors rather than forcing market share gains in an already-dominant position
Consider raising realtor marketing fees modestly, given the extremely high ROI (~740–980%) realtors currently enjoy on that spend
Explore add-on services (mortgage, title, inspections) to diversify revenue without proportional cost increases
risks: Potentially inherent differences between markets — company may lack local knowledge to replicate Seattle success
Difficult to manage more dispersed groups of realtors across cities
Exchange rate and regulatory risks in Vancouver (foreign market)
Realtor turnover if marketing fees are raised significantly
Overexposure in Seattle if continued aggressive hiring reduces average agent quality or productivity
next_steps: Research industry trends, demographics, and competitive dynamics in Portland and Vancouver
Evaluate financial capacity to open offices in new cities and hire market managers
Analyze feasibility of closing lower-performing Seattle offices to fund expansion
Conduct realtor satisfaction analysis before adjusting fee structures
Model out 5-year P&L scenarios for each expansion option using Exhibit B growth rates
